transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-05 14:00 UTC
Duration: 1h15m
Attendees: Sofia Patel (Redwood AE), Marcus Lee (Redwood SE), Evan Chu (Redwood SE), Anya Kovach (PineRiver - Head of Cloud Security), Dmitri Orlov (Infra), Priya Menon (Compliance), Lila Torres (Ops)
Links shared: Private deployment checklist (shortlink: http://rwd/priv-check), preliminary BYOK diagram (http://rwd/diagrams/byok-v1), SOC2 summary (http://rwd/artifacts/soc2-summary)

[00:00:05] Sofia: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick agenda — KMS and key rotation, egress segmentation strategy, audit logs, and then any SOC2/ISO questions. Marcus, you wanna kick us off on the KMS side?

[00:00:20] Marcus: Sure. So high-level, Redwood Private supports three modes: managed keys, BYOK via cloud KMS, and HSM-backed split-key designs. I'm gonna be a little sloppy on product names, we sometimes say Redwood Dedicate instead of Dedicated, but concept still holds.

[00:00:38] Anya: Important for us is BYOK — we have regulatory controls that require us to rotate keys under our control and show attestation. We cannot have keys fully managed off-prem where we can't revoke.

[00:00:48] Marcus: Totally. For BYOK we support envelope encryption: customer master key in your KMS (Cloud KMS or on-prem HSM), RW pods hold only data-encryption keys encrypted under that CMK. Rotation is done by creating a new CMK version and re-wrapping; we can automate rewrap with a small job or do lazy rewrap on first use.

[00:01:10] Dmitri: What about key material never touching public cloud KMS? We are evaluating an air-gapped HSM approach for PHI workloads.

[00:01:18] Evan: Yes, we have an on-prem agent model where the control plane is separated — the customer keeps keys in their HSM and we never see plaintext. You can use an offline, FIPS 140-2/3 HSM and we support an attestation workflow. There is additional ops overhead but it's supported.

[00:01:40] Priya: For SOC2 evidence we'll need rotation logs, who triggered rotation, and proof that old keys are disabled. Also retention windows for logs. Can Redwood produce hash-signed rotation records?

[00:01:55] Marcus: We emit tamper-evident audit entries. In Private we can forward logs to your SIEM via syslog or an HTTPS collector. Those logs include key rotation events with UUIDs, actor (service principal or SSO user), timestamp, and a signature blob. We can also append an HMAC envelope for added proof.

[00:02:15] Anya: Good. Now egress — we cannot allow uncontrolled egress from model hosts. We need strict allow lists and FQDN-based egress controls ideally, plus TLS interception is off the table.

[00:02:28] Marcus: Understood. Typical architecture patterns we recommend: 1) Private subnets for model hosts with no internet route; 2) Egress through a controlled gateway — either a customer-managed NAT/proxy or a dedicated egress appliance (we call it egress gateway) that sits in a hardened subnet; 3) Outbound rules limited to specific endpoints — e.g., your S3 buckets for model storage, specific telemetry collectors, and our control plane endpoints if needed.

[00:02:55] Lila: We use a forced-proxy model today — everything goes through Squid in our DMZ. Can Redwood integrate with that?

[00:03:04] Marcus: Yes, we can route egress traffic through your proxy. Two options: configure RW hosts to use the proxy via environment variables and host routing, or attach a sidecar that funnels external calls. The sidecar approach can do TLS origination so that the proxy sees only allowed endpoints. There's some nuance with streaming responses — long-lived connections need proxy keepalive tuning.

[00:03:30] Dmitri: How do we handle model downloads? We want to avoid public egress for model pulls.

[00:03:36] Evan: For model provisioning we support private model registries (private S3 endpoints, signed URLs using VPC endpoints) and also an option to pre-seed images via an offline transfer. If you want zero egress to public internet, we can set up a peered bucket or an on-prem artifact repo.

[00:03:56] Anya: Firewall levels — we need port-level rules and also application-layer filtering. Does Redwood require any inbound ports on our VPC?

[00:04:05] Marcus: For Private we typically require outbound connectivity to our control plane for health and provisioning; however, you can opt for an air-gapped mode where control plane connectivity is replaced by a manual sync (more operational). If you keep a control-plane connection, it is outbound-only on a fixed set of IPs and ports (443). Inbound to your hosts isn't required.

[00:04:25] Priya: We're leaning toward a hybrid: control plane allowed but restricted to our strict egress gateway and allow-list only.

[00:04:30] Sofia: Quick clarifying question — for SOC2 scoping, Priya, do you consider proof-of-key-ownership and rotation logs mandatory for Type II?

[00:04:38] Priya: Yes. Also we need RBAC evidence: who can promote models, who can change KMS mappings, and that role changes propagate.

[00:04:46] Marcus: We map RBAC to SAML groups via SCIM sync. You can bind actions (promote model, rotate key, change routing) to roles. We also support service principals for automation with least privilege policies.

[00:05:02] Dmitri: How granular is the RBAC — can we limit certain users to only read logs and never trigger deploys?

[00:05:09] Evan: Yes, we have fine-grained permissions at the API route level. It's not full IAM but close — read, list, deploy, manage-keys, manage-config; we can extend via SCIM groups.

[00:05:22] [00:05:40] Anya: About audit logs: retention policy — the auditors want 1 year immutable, 7 years archival for infra that touches PHI. Can Redwood support write-once logs?

[00:05:50] Marcus: We support forwarding to S3 with Object Lock (WORM) or to your internal SIEM which can provide immutability. Our local retention is configurable but for long-term you should ship logs off-cluster. We also provide signed digests of log batches if you need an additional tamper-proof layer.

[00:06:12] Lila: And what about data residency? We have EU patient data that must stay within EU regions. If model hosting is in EU, how do we ensure no accidental replication to US?

[00:06:22] Marcus: You can pin model versions to region-specific pools. Model artifacts and trained KV cache live in region. Cross-region replication is opt-in only and blocked by default. We can also disable backups off-region.

[00:06:35] Anya: Great. Can you sketch the key rotation cadence you'd recommend? We're thinking quarterly but auditors sometimes want monthly for certain PKI assets.

[00:06:44] Marcus: For CMKs a quarterly rotation is common; for data-encryption keys you can do shorter lifetimes — weekly or even per-deployment. We support two approaches: planned rotation (create new CMK version, run rewrap job) or key rotation on-demand with lazy rewrap. There's trade-off: immediate rewrap is costly for large datasets, lazy rewrap delays full compliance evidence until rewrap completes. For audits, we can produce rewrap job logs and confirm when each object was rewrapped.

[00:07:12] Priya: What about emergency key revocation? If a key is compromised, we need fast cutover.

[00:07:18] Evan: We have an emergency revoke procedure: disable the CMK, spin up a new CMK, and rewrap. However, rewrapping on a large cache can cause increased latency while items re-encrypt. We recommend pre-provisioning a secondary key and failover hooks so you can revoke quickly and keep serving against newly-wrapped keys.

[00:07:38] Dmitri: Any latency penalty for envelope encryption or HSM calls? We are latency-sensitive for inference.

[00:07:44] Marcus: Envelope encryption is cheap — DEKs are cached in memory per-worker, and HSM operations are limited to key unwrap/wrap events, not per-token. The main latency is at model invocation if you synchronous-call an external KMS for each request; we avoid that by caching and by local decrypts of DEKs. HSM-bound operations only hit at rotation or initial warmup.

[00:08:05] Anya: Okay — let's pivot to egress segmentation specifics. Our compliance requires that only DNS to internal resolvers and our telemetry to be allowed out. Everything else blocked. How have you seen customers implement this without breaking model updates?

[00:08:16] Marcus: Pattern we've used: separate control/management plane egress — only specific FQDN/IP ranges for control plane are allowed; model artifacts are pulled from a customer-controlled artifact store (VPC endpoint). For third-party telemetry we recommend a dedicated telemetry collector inside your network so outbound is only to that collector.

[00:08:32] Lila: Does Redwood support mTLS between model hosts and our internal systems?

[00:08:36] Evan: Yes, we support mTLS for all internal RPCs and service-to-service calls if you provide certs via your PKI; there's a cert rotation workflow.

[00:08:45] Priya: About firewall rules — do you require any ephemeral ports to be open? Our security team says ephemeral outbound ports are a no-go.

[00:08:53] Marcus: For streaming we open persistent TCP connections from hosts to control endpoints on 443 and keepalive; we avoid arbitrary ephemeral ranges. If you have a strict firewall that only allows 443 to specific IPs we can work with that.

[00:09:05] Anya: Can we get a diagram that maps these flows — control plane, model pulls, metrics, logs — to our network zones?

[00:09:12] Sofia: We'll include the BYOK diagram and a proposed egress gateway topology in the follow-up. Marcus, will you own that diagram?

[00:09:18] Marcus: Yep, I'll produce a version that shows: model hosts in private subnet, sidecar or proxy, egress gateway, SIEM collector, and HSM. I'll include sample iptables and proxy rules.

[00:09:27] Dmitri: A few practical things — our ops team wants automation for key rotation and an API token that can trigger rewraps.

[00:09:34] Evan: We expose an admin API endpoints for rewrap/rotate operations that can be invoked by a service principal. Those calls are audited and require an RBAC check. We can support a signed webhook from your automation system to initiate rotation.

[00:09:44] Priya: For evidence, auditors want chain-of-custody for key ops — like who triggered, when, and an approval ticket. Can Redwood push activity to our ticketing system?

[00:09:52] Marcus: We can integrate with webhooks to push events into Jira/ServiceNow, or we can forward to your SIEM which you can then correlate with tickets. We don't currently auto-create tickets but it's a straightforward webhook.

[00:10:06] Anya: Anything about SAML/SSO we should know? We have strict rules: SCIM provisioning must be locked down and deprovisioning can't be delayed more than 15 minutes after a user is disabled.

[00:10:16] Evan: We do SCIM provisioning with near-real-time sync. There's a short window if your IdP delays; we recommend hooking into your IdP's user disable webhooks for immediate enforcement.

[00:10:26] Lila: Are audit logs accessible via the Console? Our auditors want a time-limited console snapshot for evidence review.

[00:10:33] Marcus: Yes, logs are available in console and can be exported. For compliance review we usually export signed snapshots and push to your archival store. Console access can be gated by SSO + IP allowlist for the auditor session.

[00:10:45] [00:11:10] Sofia: Quick interjection — pricing/ops question I know Dmitri will care about: BYOK + HSM options typically add some overhead to monthly charges because of agent and auditing features. We shouldn't dive into hard numbers now but I will follow up with an example TCO for the hybrid pattern.

[00:11:30] Dmitri: Cool. Two small edge questions: 1) If we use an on-prem HSM, do you need a dedicated network interface to the HSM? 2) What's the recommended approach for disaster recovery of keys?

[00:11:41] Evan: 1) We can integrate over your internal network using TLS to the HSM management endpoint; some customers prefer a dedicated interface or VLAN. 2) DR: backup encrypted-wrapped keys to a separate offline vault, and ensure KMS backups are stored in a different region or an offline medium with strict access controls. We'll include a DR checklist.

[00:12:05] Priya: For the audit, can Redwood provide sample evidence packages from other customers (sanitized) for auditors to review?

[00:12:12] Marcus: We can provide templates and redacted examples of rotation logs, RBAC snapshots, and an example WORM S3 export. Not customer-identifying content, but the format should help your auditors.

[00:12:25] Anya: Great. Let's talk about timeline: we want a pilot in our EU region by end of September. That gives you time to produce the BYOK doc and for us to set up egress gateway prototype.

[00:12:36] Sofia: Sounds good. We'll aim for the lab PoC in late August / early September. I'll coordinate calendars.

[00:12:42] [Crosstalk] Lila: Also confirm — retention of raw transcripts for diagnostics?

[00:12:47] Marcus: We store operational traces for a configurable retention; for Private you control log shipping so you decide retention. By default we keep short-term traces for 30 days unless you configure longer.

[00:12:58] Anya: Anything else from the Redwood side?

[00:13:02] Evan: Just one more item — we recommend pre-provisioning a secondary key and a small rewrap window test during the lab so you can see performance impact.

[00:13:10] Sofia: Okay let's do a short recap and ownerships.

[00:13:14] Sofia: Recap — Redwood to share SOC2 artifacts and Private checklist, Marcus to produce BYOK diagram + rotation runbook, schedule lab PoC for egress gateway and key rotation, PineRiver to provide VPC details and define data residency retention targets.

[00:13:30] Dmitri: Sounds right. Thanks everyone.

[00:13:34] Priya: Thanks — appreciate the clarity.

[00:13:38] Sofia: We'll follow up with a calendar invite for the PoC and attach the diagrams. Meeting adjourned.

[00:13:44] End of recording
